title: Those who hope live differently (Spe Salvi 2)
hookLine: Benedict tells Bakhita's story of finding hope
tomorrow: a safe church or a bruised one: which would Francis pick?

lines: FOR WE ARE SAVED BY HOPE.
cards: "It'll be fine." People text it after bad news, and sometimes it lands like a shrug. Is hope just that?
A mood about the future? Benedict the Sixteenth wrote a whole letter on hope, Spe Salvi, named for Paul's words, "For we are saved by hope."
And to answer, he tells the story of a girl kidnapped by slave traders, sold, and sold again, and beaten until she bled. Her name was Josephine Bakhita.

teach.b: There are two ways to hear hope, and each has a real case.

teach.h: HOPE AS A LIFE LIVED NOW.
teach.b: One view puts the weight on the promise: eternal life, a future no one can take. That hope steadies people who can't change their situation at all.
The other view puts the weight on now: hope you can see in how someone lives this week. And it carries a fair worry. Hope that only waits can make people accept what ought to change.

Benedict knows that worry; later in the letter he answers critics who called Christian hope a private escape. His own answer is Bakhita. An Italian merchant buys her for the Italian consul, and she's taken to Italy.
There, after masters who beat her, she comes to know a completely different master. In the Venetian dialect she's learning, she calls him paron: the living God, the God of Jesus Christ.
This master, she learns, had been beaten himself, and he was waiting for her. Benedict gives her conclusion: she is loved for good, this love awaits her, and so her life is good. Her scars stayed.
Her past stayed. What changed was the reason under her days. She was baptized in Venice, became a Canossian sister, and traveled Italy urging others toward the freedom she'd found.
So which view wins? In Benedict's telling, neither alone.
The hope of being awaited is what changed how she lived now.
As he puts it in the letter's opening: the one who has hope lives differently.

how: Catholics honor Josephine Bakhita as a saint, and readers of Spe Salvi return to her story as Benedict's picture of what hope does to a life.

games.q: what does “those who hope live differently” mean?
o: hoping hard enough makes good things come true
people who hope are simply more cheerful than others
hope in God changes the way a person lives today

games.q: two views and a life — tap the pairs.
p: for we are saved by hope
a future no one can take
waiting can make people accept wrongs
Bakhita's word for her new master

s: in Spe Salvi, hope is mainly a cheerful mood that things will turn out fine
Benedict's hope is knowing you're awaited and loved, which changes how a life is lived now.
Bakhita's past and scars were erased when she found hope
her scars stayed; what changed was the reason under her days.
Bakhita called God paron, Venetian dialect for master
a different master from the ones who had beaten her.

games.q: your friend says hoping for heaven is just a way to put up with things now. what's the strongest version of her view?
o: hope that only waits can make people accept what ought to change.
anyone who hopes is naive and hasn't faced the facts.
hope is fine as long as nobody acts on it.
games.why: that's a serious worry, and Benedict takes up critics who said it. his answer is Bakhita: being awaited didn't make her passive; she spent her life urging others toward freedom.

practice: Take a pen and write one hope you hold that's bigger than this week. Under it, write one ordinary thing you'd do differently tomorrow if you knew someone was waiting for you.
If you pray, you can hold the page before God in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: Those who hope live differently. Benedict's line in Spe Salvi: hope isn't only news about later; it changes how a life is lived now.

orig.note: Latin: in hope we were saved (Romans 8:24), the first words of Benedict's letter on hope.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: hope changes life, the way it changed Bakhita's without erasing a single scar. Until tomorrow.

sources.q: For we are saved by hope.
